full_judgment:
16. Under section 79 of the Evidence Act, a Court is bound to draw the presumption that a certified copy of a document is genuine and also that the concerned officer signed it in the official character which he claimed in the said document. But such a presumption is permissible only if the certified copy is substantially in the form and purported to be executed in the manner provided by law in that manner. In other words, if the certified copy is executed substantially in the form and in the manner provided by the law, the Court raises a rebuttable presumption in regard to its genuineness. The scope of section 79 was considered in Bhinka and others vs Charm Singh, AIR 1959 SC 960. In this case, three Courts rejected the certified copy of the record-of-rights on the ground that it was not genuine on the basis of not only the internal evidence furnished by the document but also on other evidence. In this case, neither the official diary of the Patwary, who was the authorised officer to issue certified copies of the record-of-rights, was produced before the Court to prove that the prescribed procedure was followed nor the extract noted in the diary to disclose that the Patwary made any note of payment as required by law. The Indian Supreme Court held that it cannot, therefore, be said that the certified copy was issued by the Patwary in substantial compliance with the provisions of law governing such issue. It follows that the Court is not bound to draw the presumption in regard to its genuineness. It was further held that even if there was any rebuttable presumption, it was so rebutted. 

 17. In the instant case, the plaintiffs neither called the concerned officer who issued the certified copies of Exhibit Nos. 3, 5 and 7 nor took steps to prove that those Exhibits are substantially in the form and purported to be executed in the manner directed by law in that behalf. Without taking such steps, the Court is not bound to draw the presumption of genuineness of Exhibit Nos. 3, 5 and 7 under section 79 of the Evidence Act when the other side raised objection as to their admissibility at the time of tendering those in evidence. 

 The production of a certified copy of a sale deed does not, however, warrant the presumption of due execution of the original document. A party producing secondary evidence of a document is not relieved of the duty of proving the execution of the original. Even in a case where a document is Exhibited without objection the Court is to be satisfied as to the execution of the document".
